text: I. In the darkness of night, sunk, with a hardened appearance, appears the region of Kisteti with a throne of rocky cliffs. Over the dark ravine the river barks, with a heart-disturbing fury. Even the mountains have leaned over, washing face and hands in the water; many have died upon their breast, they cannot wash the blood from their bodies; it thirsts for the blood of a brother’s killer, of the man who comes along the road. I say road, though what road is it, but a narrow path upon the cliff? It is far too hard to travel, scarcely placing one foot before the other. Across the way can be seen the Kist village, like an eagle’s nest, — pleasing to behold like a woman’s bosom. Above the village sleeps the black mist, with a thoughtful expression. It listens to the surroundings, and the heart rejoices at the sight.

The guest will leave here for elsewhere tomorrow, after a little while. He will go, crossing the icy hills and ridges; he darkens, makes invisible the visible world. If he makes the hunter weep, lost on the road in the cliffs, he exalts the wolf and the thief, those who roam in the darkness.

II. From above, some unknown person rolled down a rock from the cliff; the traveler looked up and saw a high hill before him. He listens… after a little while he heard the rustling of sand. The traveler becomes alert: may the enemy not be some wretch. He watches intently, standing with his gun in hand, and sees a man trudging along with a two-pronged stick. Something black is dragging headfirst, and the sand was being stirred by it. The stranger said nothing; no word came from his mouth. The gun’s metal ring glistens, like raindrops in the morning.
– Who are you, what kind of spirit are you, what are you doing around at this time?
– Who do you want? I am a hunter; I do not see you as a trustworthy man.
– In what way am I not trustworthy? Why do you speak a false word? As if I wander, like you, in this rocky land? I too am a hunter; today, however, I was simply roaming.
“— It is the hunter’s rule, isn’t it? You still remained unattended, didn’t you?”

– This too is a duty, brother, I can barely drag my feet anymore, I have traversed the whole crag, I did not leave the ravines.  
A black mist settled over it, a strong wind arose,  
it howled at me through the ravines, like a hungry wolf.  
Before my eyes I could no longer choose the path, I was trying to fall off the cliff,  
I am a stranger, I do not know the way, and by this I was greatly tormented.

I frightened the beast in many places; I clearly heard the sound of footsteps, or when the horn of a flying chamois echoed among the cliffs. It was heart-rending; I could see nothing with my eyes, and who could speak of shooting, or killing—I no longer dared to move forward.

The unknown one came close, standing near yet far,  
“Victory!” he cried out, “Do not lament, do not be wrathful.”
– Good health to you too, brother, you leaping beast-slayer.

– Here is the beast, what are you complaining about? – he pointed to the horned, dead, horn-thrown, silent, wise chamois. – If you want, let us divide it right now, as comrades, into two; I do not want even the smallest bit more, let us share it fairly. Come with me tonight; my house is not far away. Where are you from, brother? Tell me your name too. Do not worry, God has provided food for you today as well. Your share lies in this chamois killed by me. Why are you surprised? I am not joking with you, nor flattering you to your face. Then if this is not so, why did you summon me at this time?! Shame on me, if I should deprive you of your part. What are you called? Tell me your name; by your appearance you seem to be a Khevsur.

“— My name is Nunua, brother, an exile from Chieli,” Zviadauri lied, hiding his own name. What was he to do? They knew his name; he had shed the blood of many Kists. He had cut off the right hand of many a Kist, and sent many to an untimely grave.
“Tell me your name too; I’ve truly told you mine.”

– My name is Jqola, my brother, son of Alkhastai, by lineage;  
it would not be fitting for us to speak falsely to one another.  
My house stands here at Jarega, with roof and fortress at the gate.  
Come with me tonight, and I myself will lead you.  
If I do not receive you well, then I will not receive you badly either.  
Tomorrow, you yourself know, my brother, wherever you wish, go.  
Some of my sorrow I will tell you, and some of yours you will share with me.

“Where I have not plowed, brother, there I reap” — where is that from? I’ll cut your throat for the ibex; its legs are already broken. If I come to visit you, you won’t refuse me; I’ll help you carry the ibex, and I won’t ask for a share, know that I would not stoop to that.

They skinned the beast, they went to Jarega,  
They talked much of stories, and got to know one another on the way.
III. They arrived; towers appeared, dogs bark here and there; curious children peer through the gates. The houses, built of smooth stone like cliffs, became clearly visible.
– Here is my family, my fortress and my home; come as a brother to a brother, as a godfather to a godchild – a godparent.

Joqola called to his wife: – Look out at the door! – It seems the host is in a boastful mood in conversation. They stand in the corridor, waiting… The fire flickered on the embers, he was playing the chonguri, and some timely man sat beside him. He sang of heroism, of the trials of his forefathers: how they used to raid the Pshavs and Khevsurs, not sparing the blood of their brothers; everywhere they give thanks to the right hand of a brave man.
A beautiful woman appeared, dressed in black clothes, as if girded in a siege, a star fallen from the sky.
– Here, I brought you a guest, – God’s grace is upon us, – how you receive him, woman, now depends on you.
The woman offered a greeting: – Guest, may you have arrived in peace! – Peace to you too, may you live with your husband and your share of fortune!

IV. The man who was in the house, gray-haired, old, rose to his feet too, like a mountain tiger, strong. A stranger who has come as a guest, one honors another’s guest; to stand up is the custom, one cannot break the mountain’s rule. But when he saw the stranger, he took on the color of a wolf; it was easy to tell what he was thinking. The timely Kist did not like the sight of a foreign servant. His heart beats with anger, his face does not hide it either; at times his hand goes to the dagger, quietly he tested the knife, but a guest in another’s house cannot stir up trouble. He rose and quietly went out, bit his finger bitterly, and three times struck his heart with his hand when he went outside.

Went away, goes from door to door, sharpening his tongue with poison:  
“Pshavs, our blood enemy has crept in upon us by night.  
It seems Jqola does not recognize him, has not seen with his eyes  
that one who drove us out, who ravaged us by force;  
the insatiable one, always with our blood and bones,  
today is in our hands; let us try to make him taste bitter grief.  
We have the one killed by them this summer, a masterless corpse.  
Say, if I am not speaking the truth, if my words are false?!  
Let our enemy also learn that we are not a people without lineage.  
I am amazed at Jqola’s wisdom: why did he open the door to the enemy,  
whom is the foolish one hosting, why is he not troubled in his mind?!  
We must make Zviadauri bleed from the nose with vinegar,  
otherwise let us surrender our sword and shield to the women.”

The children of the Kist were stirred,  
everyone girded on a sword;  
the whole village was stirred:  
child, man, and woman alike.  
They must offer to their dead  
the head of Zviadauri;  
they must slaughter him on the enemy’s grave,  
as is the custom.

They sent one scout, and they instructed him in secret: let him go to Jqola as a neighbor, as a brother; let him not let the village’s intention be heard by him in any way. Let him dine, converse, and learn the guest’s sleeping place; at night they will attack, seize him, and not have to wait long.

He went as a spy with a smooth-tongued manner, congratulating Jqola on his name, cheerful, not bearing offense. He jokes, tells stories, and sharpens his tongue like a whetstone. Who knows, his heart may be full of snake venom and poison.

They dined. The host likes his guest with all his heart.  
“Seems a good man,” he swears by his faith:  
“This one meeting, tomorrow brotherhood, let us unite in spirit together…”  
He invited him to sleep there, gave up his own bed.  
“No,” the guest says, “I don’t want a mattress and blanket.  
I’ll lie down in the corridor; I’m not even used to sleeping indoors…”

His desire was fulfilled, drawn out from his heart;  
this is what the listener wants,  
therefore he has been summoned here.  
He went away delighted,  
and informed everyone.  
If the fox knows the rooster’s roost,  
what more does it need?!

V. – What is the matter, woman? I want a sword and a dagger! This is no joking matter, the enemy army has fallen upon us! They intend to ravage us utterly; our guest is betraying us; with brotherhood and friendship they have slipped the host into our midst! Hush, wait!.. I was mistaken… they are our Kists. Why have they come at this time, what are they discussing, what do they want from whom?! Listen closely, I can hear a man’s rustling. What a harsh noise, what a dreadful roar! They are killing my guest, indeed, the gleam of daggers stands before them. Look at the shameless ones, how they trample my household! They have seized my honor, they are crushing it underfoot like mud; let me find out, I’ll go and see, what are they raging about, and why?!

Jokhola said this, rose, and went out with dagger in hand. He opened the house door and stepped out resolutely.  
– What are you doing? – he shouted at them: – Whose guest are you binding with a rope? Why are you breaking our sacred custom, why are you pouring disgrace upon us with a bucket? I swear by my faith, I will shed blood; I will make you regret your foolish deed, I will make you regret, though you are my brothers, trampling on my honor!..

– What are you saying, fool, what are you saying? Why do you not come to your senses? For the sake of a blood enemy guest, who would cut off a mother’s breast?! – shouted the Kists in one voice, loudly, like thunder: – You and your guest, both together, we will throw you out with a shove. Whatever the clan desires, it will do according to its clan law. Why do you keep in your house as a guest the one who drove all of Kisteti out? Even a child in the mountains knows Zviadauri’s name. This has always been so, dimwit, in the attempt to wipe us out, when he would attack us like a wolf, when he would lie in wait on our road.
Jokhola thought for a moment, a look of regret came over his face, as if the arrow that had been shot had struck him right in the hollow of the heart.

– It was he who killed your brother in the birch groves with a gun; we know that face of his, smeared over with rage. “I am Zviadauri!” he shouted to us from the hill; we know it well, plainly, for we watched him from afar. He filled Pshav-Khevsureti with cattle driven over here. The swift-footed one in a dark chokha followed after the army. Why do you dirty your head, poor soul, with the greedy pig? How can your heart not turn at sitting and staying with him?!

“— That is true, it may be… What can you tell me by that? Even so, you cannot bind my heart to your heart’s desire with a thread. Today he is my guest; even if the sea were to run with blood, still I could not betray him, I swear to God, I am made of that. I beg you, let him go, Musao, do not torment him harshly; when he leaves my family, then treat him badly there. To whom do you sell a guest? Where in Kisteti has such a thing ever been spoken of? What wrong have I done that you have come to my door? You have forgotten your own law, that is why you act wrongly; how will you answer to my family? You are in a house, are you not, and yet you make a disturbance! Woe to you, sons of the Kists, who have gathered at my door in a crowd! You torment the unarmed—what does the heart itself feel?”

Musa (to Jokhola): You too will be tied to this one, you insolent one, for breaking the face of the community! How dare you violate our decision? You have started barking like a cur, babbling foolishly like a fool; for the sake of this giaour, you even treat your brothers as enemies. Do you not know that from today your own affair will also go downhill?!

Jokhola (to Musa): What? Cur, you say? Have you now made me a dog too?! — He drew his dagger and thrust it into Musa’s heart up to the hilt. — Look at the dog himself, look how far his insolence has gone! You destroy my manhood, and yet you think you have the right to insult me too? I swear by Allah, I will crush you, I will cut you down with swords before you can finish me off; may the grace of heaven and earth be wrathful with you, for you do injustice!

– What has the godless one done, what has he done? He has gone mad, he is out of his mind… – The whole army of the Kists fell upon Jokhola, they bound his hands… they did not allow him to use his sword… bound hand and foot, they threw him into the corridor like a dead man; the people’s curse is thunder, spit is like raindrops. They brought the wounded one; Zviadauri too is in custody.

What does Zviadauri say? Why does his face look so pale?  
It is resentment that kills the brave man, because he has no sword in hand:  
“Put me in your hands, you dogs, and may fair weather be upon you.”  
This he said calmly, speaking of nothing else.  
They were taking him to the cemetery, where the Kists’ dead are;  
he is to be offered to their dead, so that there he may carry water for him,  
serve him as a servant, obediently, and wash his filthy clothes…

VI. Beyond the village, the hill is scorched, sandy.  
Many a brave man lies there, lion-hearted, of noble stock.  
Below it stretches a silent slope, washed out, clayey.  
The hard heart of the sword- and dagger-wielder, the gun-user, does not tremble;  
the earth, tongueless, cruel, and insatiable, devours them;  
in it the human countenance of everyone dissolves…  
Neither the claw of death nor deceitful words can save us.  
This is nature’s sin, my ever-sorrowful one:  
it kills both the wicked and the good, and spares no one.  
For all travelers it is swallowed up, when the ship is lost!..

VII. Here is the grave of the Kist, the people have gathered around it,  
the mullah begins the prayer, remembering his dead:
“Do not suffer, Darlao, do not trouble yourself; your brethren have come to the gate of your grave, we offer you a sacrifice too; rejoice, we will not let the enemy’s grief be your lot.”

– May your dead be a dog! – The brave man raises his voice,  
he bristles with rage, like a tiger — his hair.  
The kiln fire catches the altar’s desire.  
What can bend the brow-clouded, neck-rusted mountain!
They turn to Zviadauri, they press a sword to his throat:
“Darlasamts shaetsirebi,” everyone calls it.
“May your dead one be a dog!” — he would reply to the people.
A brave man does not bow down, nor would he furrow his brow.

The children of the Kists were astonished, the people stood on end.  
“Just look at the dog, as if he is not to be sacrificed!”¹ they cry, while slowly thrusting the sword into his throat.  
“Let him be a dog,” he said in his throat, before they cut off his head!  
“Look, just look, he does not blink an eye!”  
Life is fading, blood is flowing — Zviadauri was dying,  
the enemy’s hand could not kill his heart; his heart remained brave.  
And one woman, seeing this scene, was fainting,  
the beautiful one hid her tears, stood behind the crowd.  
She was trying to help: “Do not kill him!” her heart cries,  
furious, she thought: if only they gave me an axe,  
if only the law of womanhood allowed me,  
so that I could keep him alive and make everyone else’s souls tremble.  
If only the one who lay on his arm,  
whose breast, now cursed, touched his chest and heart!  
Would that one ever grow weary of her husband’s love?!

The Kists grew angry and insisted: they had not been able to fulfill their wish; they had not been able to prepare for their dead man the fitting meal. The slain man had slain their hearts and dashed their boasting. The insulted ones wanted to draw their daggers together and make blood-stained windows on the corpse of the dead man. But they do not dare; they are ashamed: “It is a sin!” — everyone thought. The hearts and minds of the people were moving toward regret. They said, as they turned back home, walking with their heads bowed: would we not have killed him if our enemies had not done evil? He was a good brave man, everyone swore by Allah, that is why he fought us like a tiger, defending his own land. But treat the enemy as an enemy, the Lord himself has commanded, and it is better that we try as soon as possible to drive a knife into his heart.

They went. Zviadauri was left standing there, abandoned in the desolation. Let the dogs drag him, let the birds tear him apart in common; if he was not to be sacrificed, let him lie there, that too will be enough as punishment. Thus the Kists were saying, with pride, loudly. The dark ravines echoed that same voice throughout the mountains.

The evening hour arrived, the sunbeam descended from the mountain,  
darkness is creeping in, the soul has left the light.  
They stood still, the sunbeams stood still, no longer did the sand glitter;  
no longer is seen, the white hair of the black mountain has vanished;  
the face of that rocky cliff, embroidered and woven with sorrow,  
which is always mourning, from it clear tears flow.  
Death is suited by mourning, a dead brother — a sister’s weeping,  
the forest — the flight of ox and deer, at times — the howling of the wolf.  
For a brave man — death in battle, in hand — a broken sword,  
for war — the joy of the victors and the defeat of the enemy.

Zviadaur was mourned by the turmoil and tossing of the water,  
by the sigh descending like a breeze from the high mountain.  
The tears of the army of clouds are commanded by God.  

And at the spring’s edge a woman — fair, beautiful — a Kist woman,  
pours water on her forehead and breast, and from time to time faints.  
She wept much in silence, though from time to time she would start;  
Zviadaur’s death appeared before her eyes.  

She was crying, but it was not true crying; she was ashamed:  
on one hand, she feared the honor of the clan; on the other, God frightened her;  
upon the enemy of Khevsureti’s mourner He would pour out wrath.  
This thought was of the mind, but the heart did its own will;  
the death of a man like a man did not fade from her heart.  

That image was driven into the woman’s heart like an arrow;  
it laid upon the beautiful one the mourning of the slain as a burden on her neck.  
She waits for darkness, to go and weep for the dead at night;  
she no longer thought how Jqjola might be ruined.  

Whose wife is she, whose husband does she weep for?  
What is she doing, mad with grief?!  
Perhaps they are killing Jqjola, and the house’s door has been broken open!

He rose, looking like a frightened beast; step by step he made his way along the rocky bank of the ravine; in the darkness, the water’s mournful horn sounds terribly. He passed by the grave with reverence, knelt beside the dead man, and wept with a heart full of grief; the hard stone was softened by his tears. He unsheathed the knife, turned to Zviadauri, and cut off three locks of hair with its blade as a sign, as a keepsake; with his crystal-carved fingers he wrapped them in a corner of his headcloth…

What sound is this that he hears, standing still? A wail goes through his ears… From the graves comes the wrath and lament of the dead! It is as if even the children had begun to cry, and a bitter shrieking rises! The sound of common anger is heard, common pain of heart: “What is he doing, the shameless one,” they complained in bitterness, – “May the High God be wrathful with you!” They cried out from the grave. The hurried clouds were rolling over the face of the sky.

Ran, he runs, he looks back — the dead are chasing him, that is true.  
“Where will you flee from home, if you have already been driven away from here?!”  
A voice is heard, from the pursuers; the mountain itself says the same,  
and around him, standing in wait, are they not one and two.  
“Shameless one!” cry out the upright junipers,  
the grasses, the stones, the sands, all lying in that place.  
Look, from the grave has risen his dead brother Ebari,  
unequaled among his peers, a famed horseman in Kisteti.  
And he kept crying to his sister, his words sharp as they came from his mouth:  
“Alas, sister, sister, what have you done to me? Why has fierce wrath fallen upon me?  
You have put me into a second grave, while I already lie in one tomb!  
Is that how you prove sisterhood to me, is that your womanhood?!”
A barking dog was trotting along the path toward the cemetery.

VIII. – Where will you go, where, you accursed one, where are you hurrying to?! Who will feed you with the flesh of a good man’s body? Dog, your eyes have gone stiff! Have even Zviadauri’s bones become your gnawing prey?! – said Agaza, and kept hurling stones at it again and again. She runs and follows it madly along the edge of the rocky ravine. The voice of the dead is heard again; the mountains echo it too, and Agaza’s jet-black hair also speaks reproachfully.

He approached his house, and light could be seen there;  
he should cry out, “Help me,” and make his voice reach inside.  
But he cannot say anything; sweat pours down his forehead like water.  
He arrived, breathless, and collapsed upon the threshold.

By the hearth sat Jqola, with one knee crossed over the other.  
“Alas,” he kept saying, but the words dried on his tongue.  
The husband put his arm around his wife and dragged her to the hearth.  
– What has happened to you, woman? – he asks anxiously, – I already have enough troubles; must you now become another burden for me? What has happened, what is it? Tell me, open your lips! Surely no one has tried to throw you over his arm? Tell me, I will not let you suffer for it; I will make him regret that very moment.  
I will soon bring to reason whoever has stained my honor, just as I made Musa regret going to another’s door.  
– He waited for an answer from his wife, staring down at her.  
And meanwhile he was clutching his dagger, his hand gripping the hilt.

The woman could say nothing; her face had gone pale. Jqola hovers around her, waiting to hear what his wife will say. In the middle of the night, Agaza slowly gathered her thoughts. She said to Jqola:

– “What are you saying? Why have you taken leave of your senses? Why do you think of what should not be thought of? It is all a lie… I have seen no sign of a man anywhere; who would dare do that to me, and why would I need a veil and dress?!”

“I returned from the cemetery; I was searching for your horse in the ravines, and instead of the horse, I sadly wandered among the devs.  
There met me one in a black cloak, of enormous build: even now the foulness of his skin gleams in my eyes;  
big-eared, with protruding teeth, ugly, black in color; he stretched out his hands to me, huge hands of his own, and above his head there seemed like a mountain a darkish leather hat.  
And he said to me: Come with me, live with me, woman, I have much gold and silver, I will hide nothing from you.  
I ran away, I was frightened, and the dev followed me with a roar; the whole earth shook beneath his feet with a rumbling; this voice terrified me, and even the mountains and valleys turned upside down, and with great difficulty I reached you and told you of my woe in a hoarse voice.”

Jokhola will say: – Apart from the dev there is another matter too; my mind does not believe what has been said, my thoughts are in confusion. Why are you tearful? Tears are streaming down your cheeks; speak quickly, tell me plainly, or I cannot bear it! Some sorrowful, significant feeling has flown into your heart. The trace of that feeling cannot hide from my eyes; it is impossible not to show what has been drunk, what has been poured!..

“Why should I hide it from you, Jokhola, or why would you be angered by my telling it?” his wife would say, and a gentle tremor came into her voice: “I have shed tears for that friend of yours. I felt so sorry for the poor man, dying in a foreign land, with neither kinsman nor brother to pity him! But when they were killing him with a dagger, he did not tremble at all. Perhaps I have sinned against you, and against God too, but I wept—what could I do!.."
– How could I scold you for that? It is better to tell the truth than to lie. Did you cry?! You did well; what business is it of mine? It is always fitting for a woman to mourn a good man.

IX. The next morning Agaza drove the cow toward the mountain; birds were coming down, drawn toward the dead man; Agaza too slips away toward the cliff above the cemetery. From there she startles the crows, the broad-winged vultures, the greedy eagles, clamorously circling over the dead man’s carcass; she moves her hands and hides her eyes, bright as the sun. From the cliff she throws pebbles and, at the same time, knits a stocking as if, skillfully pretending, so that people may not be able to guess her thoughts.

X. News came to Biso, like a thunderclap: “They have killed Zviadauri, the pillar descended from heaven, the shield and sword of Pshav-Khevsureti, the one most fit to be of use!” The women raised a cry upon hearing the dark news.

The old man was weeping at Biso, lamenting, sobbing bitterly: “Why am I, the wretched one, still alive? Bury me in the earth too; show me my son’s arms, bring them here, and lay me beside him! With my son’s right hand, cover my heart with earth; alas, why am I still alive? Why should I still tread these lands?! O dead ones, why did you not call me earlier to be with you? How can I bear to remember the lands of my faithless son?!”

The men heard the news, a sorrowful tale to hear,  
and spoke to one another with mouths filled with bitterness:  
“Why are you surprised, when we weep for our protector with hot tears?!”  

They brought out spears, with noses greased in tallow,  
and, adorned with shield and sword, they prepare the army at dawn.  
This is nothing new; let blood flow through the channel.  

Aparekai cries: “You want a funeral feast for Sunday!”  
“Every man must go!” — Baburauuli shouts.  
It is the turmoil of the agitated; do not think the sound is from a flute!

XI. – Come out to the door, Jokhola, do not lie quietly by the hearth,  
how many people have gathered around the peak of those mountains of ours!  
They are coming to us as guests, they are inviting us to a feast.  
They will lull mothers and children’s cradles to sleep.  
They are driving the livestock away, what a commotion it is!  
Look, the army has filled it, army leader, Sam-Gori,  
the cliffs of the shepherds who have been trampled follow in a slope.  
Go, help your own people, they are running to meet the enemy,  
you too go, Jokhola, just as the others are going.

– Shall I go with you?! What are you saying, you thin-brained fool? They won’t let me near! I must fight alone, so the whole army can see me; let the whole country see who is loyal and who is not. The Kists think I am disloyal, that I have abandoned my faith; they think Jojola sold himself for money, that I am a traitor to Kisteti, that I have thrown my soul away; they bring it and lay a gravestone on my chest while I am still alive.

This is what Joghola was saying, while he was putting on his armor:  
he girded a French sword at his waist,  
threw a rifle over his shoulder;  
for a Kist, wearing a helmet on his head is not fitting by birth.  
He goes alone to one side, devoted to the trial,  
while others have spread out on the mountain to meet the enemy.

Suddenly a Kist leapt from the cliff, sword raised high,  
astonishing the Kist host by driving back the enemy army.  
Some thought it was a trick, saying it was an apparition:  
– Who is it that meets the Khevsurs? It is our side—who is it?

– That must be Jqola, exactly, truly that is he! – said one, and the others agreed, staring in amazement. How is he not afraid of the crowd, though they brandish swords and daggers at him. They even killed him; he is falling, they are tracing his chest with the tip of a dagger.

The Kists were very pleased indeed: “Let them kill him, if they killed him — serves him right! Even now he has mocked us; before, too, he often humiliated us, he wanted to outdo the village, but instead he dragged us through the mud. He stood alone against the enemy army, and truly, by sheer luck, he scattered us.”

The Khevsur Jq'ola was left for dead, on the cliff-top, on the ledge.  
They themselves charged the Kists, and spread out down the slope.  
There came the whirling of swords and daggers, the blows went as far as the breast;  
the clashing and ringing of shields and swords rose up to the sky, to God.

They gathered the bones into a saddlebag and turned back home at once,  
they fulfilled the desire of the heart, the promise made before.  
They drove off the sheep and cattle, crossed back over the mountains;  
they vented their grief at the enemy—what sorrow is left now?!  
At least they did not leave them in a foreign land;  
they bring their dead home,  
the hope of Pshav-Khevsureti,  
the stone fortress, the iron gate.  
Their kinsmen will mourn their dead in their own custom,  
and lay them in the grave beside their forefathers:  
dearly prized is the tear that runs down one’s own chest!

XIII. – The stranger’s man, O Mozarev, the Khevsurs have killed your husband. Go, weep, Agaza, and commit him to the grave. The raven will flutter above him, and the wind will comb his beard and mustache.

– May your enemy have such a life, for my life is miserable! No one comes near me anymore, no one lends me a shoulder. I buried him right there on the top of the cliff, and I dug him a grave; everyone has turned their backs on me, everyone stands aside. Even the cemetery was closed to me, so I could bury the body: “Jokhola betrayed us,” they say, “that is the place for him, where he fought alone, the one who brought disgrace upon us, the breaker of the community’s honor, faithless, restless.” Fire burns me, brother, fire burns me, without flame, unkindled; it is killing my heart, confusing my mind with incomprehensible thoughts!

The wife wept for Jokola,  
often shedding tears,  
like a chamois with its neck thrown back,  
with thick hair, moon-faced,  
she clung to her husband’s chest  
like a pearl button.

XIV. It is a dark night, there is a storm, the surroundings are rumbling.  
God, look upon the suffering, help them, have mercy!  
At least let the good be good — gather the poor ones together!  
Let the prayer and supplication of the suffering be laid upon the heart like roses!  
If You do not help, gather up the souls of the wretched!..  
Enough of that much threat, cloud, scatter away!

The river roars, rages,  
it surges over the rocks;  
today it is just as wicked,  
it does not know why it laments.  

It does not fear suffering,  
it does not know death.  
It knows only one thing:  
to shed tears, to cry out loudly,  
everlasting sorrow,  
to weep alone, to weep…

– Why should I live, for what purpose? the woman was thinking. – Even my faithful little stone is nowhere in Kisteti. We both sinned against the Kists; they showed me a husband… I have the greater sin, for I have shed tears for a stranger.
The water carried away the agaza, the mud, and the sand.

XV. On the cliff where Jqola was killed in the Khevsur fight, they see at night an image in the avalanche-piled hill: Jqola stands on the cliff and calls toward the cemetery: “Zviadaur, my brother, why do you not show me your face?!” From the cemetery comes a shadow, armed with shield and sword, with folded arms on his chest, wearing armlets. He comes and silently greets his brother-friend. There too Agaza rises, her face sorrowful, mournful. A fire burns beside them, faintly flickering on the mountain; Agaza hosts them there, roasting deer kebabs over the flame. They speak of manliness, of mutual trust, and of the customs of host and guest, and of brotherhood and sisterhood.

When a man sees them together, he cannot get enough of looking; but then there appears a kind of mist, black in color like soot, and it covers the view with the writing of a scribe. It hangs over them like a spell, it cannot be broken with a hammer, nor can a prayer be cast off by one who prays, nor can it be lifted by hand.
Only the sound of the river is heard; below, with a cough, it sways and gazes into the abyss, with the throat of the one with the primrose bent back…
